scenes.name: El oficio: del air guitar al dios del metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El músico de heavy sale del público: es el fan que toca la guitarra de aire en el concierto de UFO de 1979 y quiere estar donde está Michael Schenker. No hay escuela ni beca: hace falta talento musical y dramático (actuar la emoción por trescientas veces), un cuerpo joven y atlético (correr y pesas en la gira, el pelo largo como signo de autenticidad) y aprender a vivir en un grupo que no es ni familia ni oficina, con sus «problemas de ego» por la rivalidad entre cantante y guitarrista. El heavy es el estilo más caro de montar y casi no hay clubes donde empezar; el código exige temas propios y autenticidad. Firmar con un sello convierte a la banda en una empresa del capitalismo tardío frente a un oligopolio. El ciclo es componer, grabar (paciencia; el primer disco de Black Sabbath se hizo en doce horas, Spreading the Disease de Anthrax en cinco meses) y girar (aguante: esperar, esperar). La recompensa no es el dinero sino el carisma del chamán que alcanza el éxtasis dionisíaco ante miles de personas; el precio, «quemarse o apagarse», porque nadie que viva lo bastante puede cumplir el código.

scenes.name: Rush, Queensrÿche y el metal progresivo
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Grupos muy apreciados por la subcultura por sus letras elocuentes y cargadas de sentido, una excepción en un género que no privilegia las palabras. El trío canadiense Rush, con letras del batería Neil Peart, es el ejemplo: Weinstein pasó una noche de 1982 en el aparcamiento de un estadio explicando a sus fans la historia de 2112, una teocracia que aplasta a quien quiere hacer su propia música; muchos se sabían las letras de memoria, pero más del 70 % creía que Rush estaba del lado de los sacerdotes. Geoff Tate, de Queensrÿche, es uno de los cantantes más alabados.

podcast.title: Attempt to Break into UK Music Scene
podcast.body: At 18 years old in 1970, Neil Peart moved to England with the ambition of entering its vibrant music scene. Although this attempt did not result in a musical breakthrough, he gained valuable experience and learned a lot. By 1972, approximately 18 months later, he returned home to St. Catharines, where he worked at his father's farm equipment dealership while continuing to play in local bands. "Neil moved to England to see if you could get involved in the music scene there. That didn't work out, but he learned a lot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diverse Interests
podcast.body: Beyond his musical contributions, Neil Peart harbored a wide range of intellectual and personal interests. He had a profound love for motorcycles and a passion for big band music. He was also a hockey fan, enjoyed reading books extensively, and was dedicated to studying philosophy. "He loved to read books and study philosophy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drumming Style Evolution and Lessons
podcast.body: In 1994, Neil Peart sought further drumming instruction from teacher Freddie Gruber, an experience that significantly refined his technique. He altered his stick-holding method, adopted different movements, and evolved his playing style, often discovering that "less was more." This refinement contributed to his highly musical approach to drumming, which extended beyond mere timekeeping to include a wide array of percussion instruments and fluid movements. "In 1994, he went back to taking lessons from a teacher named Freddie Groober."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Drumming Beginnings
podcast.body: Neil Peart was born in Hamilton on September 12, 1952, and his first home was on the family dairy farm near Hager'sville. He started drumming at an early age, reportedly using chopsticks on his sister's playpen. The family later moved to St. Catharines, where at age 13, Neil began taking formal drum lessons using practice pads. After a year of committed practice, his parents bought him his first proper red drum kit. "Neil apparently liked to drum chopsticks on his sister's playpin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Influences
podcast.body: While growing up and playing in local bands, Neil Peart was deeply influenced by prominent drummers across different genres. He admired Keith Moon of The Who, Ginger Baker of Cream, John Bonham of Led Zeppelin, and Mitch Mitchell of The Jimi Hendrix Experience. Additionally, he was fascinated by big band drummers such as Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich. "He loved Keith Moon of the Who, ginger baker of cream, John Bonham of Zeppelin, and Mitch Mitchell of Jimmy Hendrix's groove."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Glioblastoma Diagnosis and Private Battle
podcast.body: Neil Peart, the drummer for Rush, was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a highly aggressive and incurable form of brain cancer, which he battled for three and a half years. He first suspected something was wrong in June 2016, less than a year after Rush's retirement, when he began struggling with the New York Times crossword puzzle, followed by issues with words a couple of months later. "Neil Pirates of Rush survived for three and a half years with his case of glioblastoma."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Health Struggles and Retirement from Touring
podcast.body: Neil Peart faced significant health challenges late in his career, including arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, chronic tendonitis, shoulder problems, and lower back issues—common ailments for hard-hitting drummers. A severe foot infection made playing Rush's R-42R tour very painful. He initially resisted embarking on this final tour, agreeing only after being persuaded, stating, "one more time and then I'm out." His last show was in Los Angeles on August 1st, 2015, after which he announced his retirement from Rush and from drumming entirely. "Neil hadn't been well, but it was all about arthritis and carpal tunnel, two things that hard-hitting drummers often suffer after years behind the kit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joining Rush
podcast.body: Neil Peart formally became a member of Rush on July 29th, 1974, a date which coincided with Geddy Lee's 21st birthday. He secured the position after auditioning, replacing founding drummer John Rutsey. His first gig with the band was shortly after, on August 14th, 1974, in Pittsburgh, where Rush opened for Uriah Heep and Manfred Mann. "He got the job and formally became a member of Rush on July 29th, 1974, which just happened to be Gettie Lee's 21st birthday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Medical Confirmation and Prognosis
podcast.body: An MRI confirmed Neil Peart's glioblastoma diagnosis, leading to surgery. Upon receiving the diagnosis, doctors initially gave him an 18-month prognosis. Despite a short period of remission, the cancer returned, and he ultimately lived twice the expected duration, dying on January 7, 2020. His battle with the disease was kept entirely private until his death. "There was an MRI which confirmed things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personal Tragedies and Temporary Retirement from Rush
podcast.body: The late 1990s were an exceptionally difficult period for Neil Peart, leading to a temporary retirement from Rush. On August 10, 1997, his 19-year-old daughter, Selina, died in a single-car accident while driving to university. Just five months later, his common-law wife of 23 years, Jackie, passed away from cancer. This double trauma prompted him to temporarily step away from the band to cope, embarking on a motorcycle tour across North America to help process his grief. "An August 10th, 1997, Neil's 19 year old daughter, Selina, died in a single car accident."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Personality and Public Persona
podcast.body: Despite his powerful and loud drumming style, Neil Peart was known as the "quiet one" within Rush, often described as an introvert and a "reluctant drumming institution." He maintained a very private life, with interviews being rare, and fan meet-and-greets typically handled by Alex Lifeson and Geddy Lee. He was highly articulate, extremely well-read, a deep thinker, and possessed a wicked sense of humor, earning unending respect for his abilities as a drummer, lyricist, and writer. "For someone who played so loud and so hard, Neil was the quiet one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Trauma Writing Career and Remarriage
podcast.body: Following his temporary retirement from Rush due to personal tragedies, Neil Peart entered a new phase of his writing career. He produced memoirs, novels, book reviews, essays, and later, blogs, with books being a favorite subject on his website under the heading "Bubba's Book Club." He also became widely known as an avid motorcyclist. This hiatus proved beneficial, as he remarried to Kerry in 2000 and subsequently returned to Rush to record the *Vapor Trails* album in 2001. "The result was a new phase of his writing career, with memoirs, novels, book reviews, essays, and soon after blogs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Private Battle with Brain Cancer
podcast.body: Sometime in 2016, Neil Peart was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer that he battled for over three years. His illness was kept entirely private, with family, friends, and management closing ranks to respect his privacy. He passed away quietly on January 7, 2020, at the age of 67. The announcement of his death was delayed until January 10, maintaining a low-key and dignified farewell, true to his introverted nature. "sometime in 2016, Neil was diagnosed as having brain cancer. He battled it for more than three years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reflections on Drumming as an Athlete
podcast.body: In December 2015, Neil Peart authored an article for *Drumhead* magazine titled "Neil Peart Reflects on 50 Years of Hitting Things with Sticks," where he discussed the physically demanding nature of his craft. He acknowledged drumming as largely an "athletic undertaking" and recognized that, like all athletes, there comes a time to step away from the game. He preferred to retire rather than face the decline described in Rush's song "Losing It" from the 1982 *Signals* album. "The reality is that my style of drumming is largely an athletic undertaking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rush Audition and Unique Appearance
podcast.body: In 1974, Neil Peart auditioned for Rush as one of five drummers, replacing founding member John Rutsey who was leaving due to health issues and a musical mismatch. At the audition, Alex Lifeson and Geddy Lee initially found Neil's appearance "goofy" because he had short hair during a time when long hair was fashionable. He also brought an unusual Slingerland double bass drum kit, notable for its unusually small bass drums. "Alex and Gettie thought Neil looked goofy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Drummer for Hire and Unique Kit
xref.body: In 1942, Viola Smith became a drummer for hire, distinguished by her skill and her elaborate drum kit, which included a couple of timpani, multiple tom-toms, an oversized kick drum, and large gong drums mounted high on either side of her head. Her setup was so impressive it was compared to Neil Peart's. "she had a huge kit with a couple of timpani's, multiple tom-toms, an oversized kick drum, and big gong drums mounted up high on either side of her head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

xref.title: Drumming Influences
xref.body: Taylor Hawkins' drumming style was heavily influenced by progressive rock drummers such as Neil Peart of Rush, Stewart Copeland of The Police, and Phil Collins during his time with Genesis. Other influences included Stephen Perkins of Jane's Addiction, Ringo Starr, and his hero, Roger Taylor of Queen. "His heroes were Neil Pirate of Rush, Stuart Copeland of the police, and Phil Collins when he was with Genesis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embraced Modern Electronic Drums
xref.body: Will Champion of Coldplay is among the contemporary drummers who have embraced modern electronic drums. These kits are used to trigger a variety of sounds, tones, patterns, and samples to suit their musical needs. "Today's electronic drums have been embraced by players such as Danny Carey, Neil Peart, Will Champion of Coldplay, Rob Borden of Lincoln Park, and many, many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Embraced Modern Electronic Drums
xref.body: Rob Borden of Lincoln Park is one of the contemporary drummers who has adopted modern electronic drums. These instruments are utilized to trigger sounds, tones, patterns, and samples, demonstrating their versatility in modern music production and performance. "Today's electronic drums have been embraced by players such as Danny Carey, Neil Peart, Will Champion of Coldplay, Rob Borden of Lincoln Park, and many, many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

xref.title: Neil Peart as an Idol
xref.body: Dave Grohl identifies Rush drummer Neil Peart as a significant influence, stating that Peart was "my guy on the wall" when discussing his early musical heroes. This highlights the impact of Peart's drumming on Grohl's own musical development and appreciation. "Meal Perk was my guy on the wall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Neil Peart's Drumming Influence
xref.body: Taylor Hawkins credits Neil Peart's drumming from Rush records for influencing "any crazy fill" he performs on the drums. This highlights Peart's lasting impact on Hawkins' percussive style within the Foo Fighters. "A lot of like anything weird that I do on the drums is usually ripped off from a rush record, like any crazy fill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Uncertain Future Post-Taylor Hawkins' Death
xref.body: The Foo Fighters face an uncertain future following the death of Taylor Hawkins, who was considered irreplaceable due to his chemistry and friendship with Dave Grohl and his essential role in the band's "family nature." Comparisons are drawn to Led Zeppelin, which disbanded after John Bonham's death, and Rush, which retired after Neil Peart's death. "What do the Fufighters do now? We don't know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: YouTube Drum Cover Artist
xref.body: Mettal Cohen is a highly skilled drum cover artist featured on YouTube. She is known for her exceptional ability to cover complex drum parts, specifically excelling at reproducing Neil Peart's intricate drumming from bands like Rush or Tool. "Metal Cohen is really, really good. She kills it when covering Neil Peiritz parts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
